1. 
Understanding Massachusetts v. EP A. At one level, Massachusetts v. 
EP A is a classic illustration of the indeterminacy of the Supreme Court’s 
standing analysis when the plaintiffs injury, the defendant’s relationship to 
that injury, and the possibility that judicial judgment will redress it, involve 
either inaction or action by an agency directed at someone other than the 
plaintiff. In all such cases, the effects on the plaintiff are indirect and can be 
described as more or less “speculative.” But EPA did not really dispute the 
National Research Council (NRC) studies’ finding that human activity was 
contributing to global warming and that global warming would produce rises 
in the level of the sea. The majority, therefore, took it as inevitable that the 
failure to prevent some contribution to global warming by air pollution 
regulation would have some impact on the State of Massachusetts’s riparian 
interests. Emphasizing the uncertainties in the chain of causation, which also 
could be found in the NRC Report, Chief Justice Roberts compares the 
majority’s opinion to the somewhat discredited SCRAP decision. And, on one 
interpretation of Massachusetts v. EPA, there were five members of the Court 
who were willing to return to the relaxed SCRAP approach. The case can, 
therefore, be viewed as in some sense validating the “public action,” a review 
proceeding in which marginally affected parties are permitted to raise legal 
issues of great moment to the pubUc at large.
2. 
Protecting Procedural Rights? But other interpretations of 
Massachusetts v. EPA are clearly available. Justice Stevens’s discussion of 
standing begins with the suggestion that the State of Massachusetts is 
defending a procedural right under the Clean Air Act, which Justice ScaBa 
seems to beheve lowers the requirements of immediacy and redressability. 
This is how Justice Scalia, for the majority in Lujan v. Defenders of Wildlife, 
described procedural rights:
There is much truth to the assertion that “procedural rights” are 
special: The person who has been accorded a procedural right to 
protect his concrete interest can assert that right without meeting all 
the normal standards for redressability and immediacy. Thus, under 
our case law, one hving adjacent to the site for proposed construction 
of a federally hcensed dam has standing to challenge the licensing 
agency’s failure to prepare an environmental impact statement, even 
though he cannot estabhsh with any certainty that the statement will 
cause the hcense to be withheld or altered, and even though the dam 
will not be completed for many years.
